title: Rajkummar Rao Gained 10 Kilos to Become the Man Who Sent Kasab to the Gallows. The Prahaar Teaser Is a Gut-Punch.
excerpt: Attached to Cocktail 2's prints and dropped online Friday, the first look at 'Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story' trades horror-comedy charm for a courtroom that still smells of cordite. Stree's golden boy has never looked heavier, or hungrier.
body:
The teaser opens not with a gavel, but with a man straightening his black advocate's band in a mirror — and the face looking back is one you almost don't recognise. Rajkummar Rao, the wiry, boyish charmer of Stree and Newton, has vanished. In his place stands a thickset, grey-templed lawyer with the heavy stillness of someone who has stared down monsters for a living. That man is Ujjwal Nikam, and Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story is the film that finally puts India's most famous prosecutor on the big screen.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=YS1k4THZjAI

The teaser slipped into cinemas this Friday attached to the prints of Cocktail 2 — a sly bit of counterprogramming, given both films come from the same producer, Dinesh Vijan of Maddock Films — before landing online and lighting up timelines by Friday afternoon. At one minute and fifty-seven seconds, certified U/A 16+ by the censor board on June 8, it is less a trailer than a warning shot. Hard-hitting dialogue, the spectre of the 26/11 trial, and Rao's transformed silhouette do all the heavy lifting.

And what a transformation. Rao has spoken openly about the physical toll: he piled on nine to ten kilos for the part, a regime he described, with characteristic deadpan, as "two pizzas, lots of sweets, aloo parathas, and biryani." The vanity-free commitment shows in every frame. This is not a movie star playing dress-up; it is an actor disappearing into a man the whole country watched on the news.

"Born in Jalgaon in 1953, Nikam built a fearsome record across the 1993 Bombay serial blasts, the Shakti Mills gang-rape case, the Gulshan Kumar murder, and most recently the Badlapur assault case."

!Ujjwal Nikam — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

"The face looking back in the mirror is one you almost don't recognise."

For those who need the refresher: Ujjwal Nikam is the special public prosecutor who secured the death sentence for Ajmal Kasab, the lone surviving gunman of the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. Born in Jalgaon in 1953, Nikam built a fearsome record across the 1993 Bombay serial blasts, the Shakti Mills gang-rape case, the Gulshan Kumar murder, and most recently the Badlapur assault case. He carries Z-plus security and a Padma Shri for his trouble. If ever a life demanded a courtroom drama, it is his — and director Avinash Arun, the cinematographer-turned-filmmaker behind Paatal Lok and the aching Three of Us, is precisely the kind of restrained, texture-obsessed storyteller who can resist the urge to turn it into a flag-waving shout-fest.

The ensemble is stacked. Jaideep Ahlawat, fresh off a run as one of the most quietly menacing actors working today, joins the cast alongside Wamiqa Gabbi — reuniting with Rao after this year's Bhool Chuk Maaf — and Sikandar Kher. On paper, it is the sort of lineup that makes a film feel like an event before a single full trailer has dropped.

For the diaspora, Prahaar lands at an interesting moment. Maddock has become the studio that exports India's most reliable theatrical events — the Stree universe, Chhaava — and a courtroom drama rooted in 26/11 carries a particular charge for NRIs who watched those three days in November 2008 unfold from living rooms in New Jersey, Leicester and Brampton. This is shared national trauma, and a film that revisits the legal reckoning will travel.

Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story opens in cinemas worldwide on August 7, 2026, with overseas distribution expected through the same theatrical chains that carry Maddock's titles in the US, UK and Canada. It arrives exactly one week before Rajkumar Santoshi's Partition epic Batwara 1947 (August 14) — making early August a heavyweight bout of Hindi cinema, prestige drama versus period spectacle.

And Rao is only getting started on his biopic run. He is also currently shooting Vikramaditya Motwane's film on former India captain Sourav Ganguly — meaning that within a year, the most chameleonic actor of his generation will have inhabited both a terror-trial prosecutor and the Prince of Kolkata. On the evidence of this teaser, betting against him would be a mistake. He's never been better.
